rule: decision 47: a mapping the blind verifier did not confirm is held — never shown, never a diagnosis, never S5 evidence — until a human keeps or drops it

items.stem: Find the set of ordered pairs (x, y) which satisfy the relation $y = 2x - 1$ when $x = 0$, $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. Tap the pairs that satisfy the relation.
items.construction: Use the targets form. Tap (3,5) and (5,3) on the board (x -1..6, y -1..6). Both are lattice points in range. The two points are different, which answers the question.
items.predicate_meaning: Selected pairs that are not in X×Y at all
items.hint: Substitute each x into $y = 2x - 1$ and compute y. Only a pair whose y matches that result belongs in the set.
items.why: It is in the can_emit table for relation mode. It fires when the student taps a pair of X×Y that the rule leaves out, such as (0,1). The hint's description says 'not in X×Y at all', which is wrong: these pairs are in X×Y, they just fail the rule. The hint text itself is mathematically right and doesn't give the answer. But it says 'Only a pair whose y matches that result belongs', which nearly directs the student to the answer. The mismatch between the predicate description and the situation makes this a risky hint, so it is rejected.

items.stem: Represent the ordered pairs (3, 5) and (5, 3) graphically in the coordinate plane. Tap each point. Are they the same point?
items.construction: Tap lattice points (3,5) and (5,3). Both lie within the board (x -1..6, y -1..6) and the set is graded order-free, so this is a correct answer.
items.predicate_meaning: Right distances, wrong signs — the point is in the wrong quadrant
items.hint: Both numbers in each pair are positive, so both moves go right along x and up along y.
items.why: It cannot fire on this board. Reflecting the targets gives points like (-3,5) or (3,-5), and the board runs only from -1 to 6, so those points cannot be tapped. The hint also reveals that both numbers are positive, which is part of the answer.

items.stem: If $X=\{1,2,3\}$, $Y=\{12,21,47,52\}$ and R is the relation from X to Y where a R b means: a is a digit of b, for each $a\in X$, $b\in Y$. Represent R by an arrow diagram: tap an element of X, then the element of Y it is related to.
items.construction: Draw five arrows: 1→12, 1→21, 2→12, 2→21, 2→52. Element 3 gets no arrow (it is a digit of none of 12, 21, 47, 52) and 47 receives none. This satisfies the limit of at most 12 pairs.
items.predicate_meaning: Arrows drawn the wrong way round — from the second element of a pair to the first
items.hint: Arrows go from the element of X (the first in the pair) to the element of Y (the second).
items.why: X and Y are different sets and the student taps X first and then Y, so an arrow cannot be drawn from Y to X. Reversal can only occur for a relation on one set, so the predicate cannot fire here and the hint would never be shown.

items.stem: Represent graphically the function $\ell(x) = -2x$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
items.construction: Equation mode, y = -2x. Drag handles to lattice points (0,0) and (1,-2) (or (-1,2)); the line through them has m=-2, b=0. Neither is at the starting handle positions (-3,-2) or (1,1), and all within the default ±5 board.
items.predicate_meaning: Slope taken as run over rise instead of rise over run
items.hint: Use your table: for each step of 1 to the right, how many units does the line move up or down?
items.why: Fires with m=-1/2 (e.g. (0,0),(2,-1)), but the hint says 'Use your table' and this question has no table, so the student has nothing to refer to.

items.stem: Represent graphically the function $\ell(x) = -2x$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
items.construction: Equation mode, y = -2x. Drag handles to lattice points (0,0) and (1,-2) (or (-1,2)); the line through them has m=-2, b=0. Neither is at the starting handle positions (-3,-2) or (1,1), and all within the default ±5 board.
items.predicate_meaning: A vertical line, which has no slope and cannot be written y = mx + c
items.hint: Each x has exactly one image, so the graph cannot be vertical. Use the table of pairs.
items.why: Can fire (two points with the same x), and the reasoning about one image per x is right, but it points to 'the table of pairs', which this question doesn't provide.

items.stem: Represent graphically the function $f(x) = 5$. Drag the two points so the line is the graph.
items.construction: Equation mode, m=0, b=5 on the default board (−5..5). Drag the handles to (-1,5) and (2,5), which are lattice points on y=5. Neither is at the starting positions (-3,-2) or (1,1), and the pipeline rule only restricts points mode. Any two points with y=5 are accepted. m=0 is a whole number and b=5 is within −5..5, so the spec is valid.
items.predicate_meaning: A vertical line, which has no slope and cannot be written y = mx + c
items.hint: Every x has the same image, so the points have different x but the same y. Does that give a vertical line?
items.why: It can fire when both points share an x. But the hint says every x has the same image and that the points need different x and the same y. That is the construction of the answer, a horizontal line, so it gives the answer away.

It is mathematically wrong and would confuse a student who built a vertical line.
